title: Footprinting and Reconnaissance
sections: Footprinting Tasks using Advanced Tools and AI

objectives.text: Tell passive from active footprinting and name the organization, network and system information it looks for
Recognize what search operators such as site:, filetype:, intitle: and inurl: return, and what the GHDB catalogs
Say what Shodan, certificate transparency logs, archives, job ads and financial filings reveal about an organization
Explain how social media exposes staff, roles and e-mail formats, and recognize theHarvester and Sherlock
Read WHOIS and RDAP data, know TCP 43 and the five RIRs, and pick the right registry for domains and IP ranges
Know what each DNS record type reveals, why open zone transfers are a problem and how TSIG and split-horizon DNS fix it
Interpret traceroute output and e-mail headers (Received order, SPF, DKIM, DMARC results)
Name the social engineering techniques used to gather information and the verification and disposal controls against them
Match footprinting tools to their purpose (Maltego, Recon-ng, SpiderFoot, FOCA, ExifTool, HTTrack) and state the limits of AI-assisted OSINT
objectives.section: Footprinting Tasks using Advanced Tools and AI

objectives.text: Choose countermeasures for each exposure and explain why robots.txt is not access control

readingMap.why: Passive versus active is the most tested distinction in the module.
Expect questions that show an operator combination and ask what it finds.
Shodan, CT logs and job postings each map to a typical question.
Know what staff profiles leak and the two tool names.
Port 43, RDAP, the five RIRs and redaction are easy points.
Record types and zone transfers come up often, including command output.
tracert versus traceroute defaults and reading Received headers are classic traps.
Mostly definitions; M9 covers social engineering in depth.

readingMap.section: Footprinting Tasks using Advanced Tools and AI
readingMap.why: Tool-to-purpose matching, plus the new v13 AI topic.
Countermeasures follow from each exposure; remember the robots.txt trap.

labs.name: Footprint your own domain from public sources
labs.skill: Looking up the registration data, name servers and certificate transparency entries of a domain you own, and listing what they expose

labs.name: Query DNS records of a domain you control
labs.skill: Using dig and nslookup on your own domain to read A, MX, NS, SOA and TXT records, and confirming your server refuses zone transfers

labs.name: Read and strip metadata from your own documents
labs.skill: Running ExifTool on documents and photos you created to see author, software and GPS fields, then removing them before publishing

labs.name: Trace the headers of a message in your own mailbox
labs.skill: Opening the full headers of a message you received, reading the Received lines bottom-up and interpreting the SPF, DKIM and DMARC results

feynmanPrompts: Explain to a small-business owner the difference between passive and active footprinting, and why most of what an attacker learns about them never shows up in their logs.
Explain why a DNS server that answers zone transfers to anyone is a problem, and how restricting transfers and split-horizon DNS reduce what the outside world sees.
Explain to a new colleague what WHOIS/RDAP records, certificate transparency logs and job postings each reveal about a company, and one countermeasure for each.
